svg.title: P028. How five orders become payment-type shares
svg.desc: Blue shows Orders. Green shows Payments. Five orders survive the left join. Orders 13 and 14 share the Unknown label. UPI has two of five orders and 300 out of 800 in value. The Unknown group has two orders worth 200. Card has one order worth 300.
svg.text: Where do 40% of orders and 37.5% of value come from?
Follow orders 10–14 from the payment lookup to their shares of the entire report.
5 order rows → 5 joined rows → 3 payment types → 2 overall denominators

g.text: The report measures transactions. OrderID identifies one transaction, including one with a missing payment method.
Orders 10–12 are the original sample. Our practice example adds order 13 for 50 and order 14 for 150.

g.aria-label: Step 2. Why LEFT JOIN on PaymentID?
g.text: Add Payments second to name each order’s payment method. A LEFT JOIN keeps orders 13 and 14 when no label matches.
Order 13 has payment ID 99. Order 14 has a missing ID. Both keep their blue order values and receive green NULLs.

g.aria-label: Step 3. Why name missing payment types before grouping?
g.text: Why name missing payment types before grouping?
The report needs one label for every order. A missing lookup becomes Unknown.
Orders 13 and 14 now have the same display label. Grouping by the original order-side payment ID would split them.

g.aria-label: Step 4. Why group by the displayed payment type?
g.text: Why group by the displayed payment type?
One report row represents one payment type. First collect the order IDs and amounts that belong to each label.
Orders 10 and 11 belong to UPI. Orders 13 and 14 belong to Unknown. Each order is in exactly one group.

g.aria-label: Step 5. Why count order IDs and add order amounts?
g.text: Why count order IDs and add order amounts?
One measure counts transactions. The other measures the money collected by that payment type.

g.aria-label: Order IDs and amounts read by each aggregate
g.text: Order IDs and amounts read by each aggregate
UPI counts orders 10 and 11 and adds 100 + 200. Card reaches the same value of 300 with one order.

g.aria-label: Step 6. Why do both scalar subqueries read all five orders?
g.text: Why do both scalar subqueries read all five orders?
A payment type’s share needs a total for the whole report. Each scalar subquery returns one number that every group uses.

g.aria-label: All five rows contribute to the denominators
g.text: All five rows contribute to the denominators

g.aria-label: The same two totals for every group
g.text: The same two totals for every group
Five order rows give a count of 5. Their amounts add to 100 + 200 + 300 + 50 + 150 = 800.

g.aria-label: Step 7. Why do the two shares use different denominators?
g.text: Why do the two shares use different denominators?
Compare a group’s order count with all orders and its value with all order value. Round each percentage to two decimal places.
UPI’s two contributions are dark blue. Read the top segments as order IDs and the bottom as amounts.
UPI has 2 of 5 orders, or 40.00%. Its 300 out of 800 in value gives 37.50%.

g.aria-label: Step 8. Why sort by the number of orders?
g.text: Why sort by the number of orders?
The payments team wants the most-used methods first. UPI and Unknown tie at two orders, so either may appear first.
The rows account for 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 orders and 300 + 200 + 300 = 800. Both shares sum to 100.00% in this example.
